narrative:
The model estimated a 59.7% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a slightly-more-likely-than-not risk, not a certainty, but it was high enough that your application was denied under the school’s screening rule.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: you were in the lowest decile, compared with an accepted-student average around the sixth decile. That low standing pushed the prediction toward failure more than any other factor. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.80 was the next most influential factor; because it is well above the accepted average of about 3.23, it pushed toward passing and was a genuine strength. However, your first-year class standing was also in the lowest decile, versus an accepted average near the sixth decile, and it added further weight toward failure. Together, the two very low class standings outweighed the positive signal from your GPA.

To improve your position, speak with an admissions adviser about whether extenuating circumstances affected your class standing, and ask what evidence would best show readiness. Consider delaying reapplication until you can strengthen your academic record, and retake the LSAT, since your score of 28 is below the accepted average of 37.18, if you can improve it. A revised application should directly address the early academic concerns and highlight sustained improvement.
